tagline: Steep canyon grades lead to lava fields and a lake draining underground
intro: SR 14 climbs through Cedar Canyon on extended grades over 8 percent, then twists through aspen and pine along the edge of the Markagunt Plateau. Utah DOT describes this state scenic byway as a 40-mile drive through Cedar Canyon and Dixie National Forest, allowing an hour between Cedar City and Long Valley Junction. The highway reaches 9,900 feet before rolling east into lava country.

The Cedar City–Long Valley Junction road entered the state highway system in 1912 and received the number SR 14 in the 1920s. A branch to Cedar Breaks joined it in 1927; that branch later became part of SR 148. Maintaining the canyon passage has meant rebuilding after landslides: one in 1989 closed the highway for months, and another in 2011 closed it for more than seven months.

The highway begins at SR 130 in central Cedar City, linking the city to US 89 at Long Valley Junction. Driving east, you leave Cedar City through its red hill and maple and scrub oak forest, then climb the narrow canyon. Beyond the summit and Cedar Breaks turnoff come lava fields, the Navajo Lake overlook and Duck Creek Village. The final descent curves through scrub oak and maple into Long Valley, ending at US 89.

moments.title: Cedar Canyon
moments.text: Sheer cliffs flank the narrow canyon as SR 14 climbs toward the plateau, with views into the Ashdown Gorge Wilderness Area. Several extended stretches of the climb exceed an 8 percent grade. The passage has a history of interruption. On October 8, 2011, a mountainside near mile marker 8 gave way, removing about 1,300 feet of road. The highway remained closed for more than seven months, reopened to limited traffic on May 12, and fully reopened on August 4, 2012. Beyond the canyon, the drive passes the Southern Utah University Mountain Center and Wood’s Ranch Recreation Area.
moments.notice: Cliffs rise on both sides of the narrow canyon.

moments.title: Navajo Lake
moments.text: A sharp bend on SR 14 brings the Navajo Lake overlook into view; the forest road down to the lake lies a mile farther east. The lake formed when lava flowed across the valley’s eastern end, blocking its drainage. People later added to the dam. Only 25 feet deep at its deepest, the lake drains through sinkholes in its floor into two drainage systems: the Great Basin and the Colorado River. Along the highway east of the Cedar Breaks junction, ancient lava fields and layers of volcanic rock mark the landscape. Elsewhere on the plateau, lava flows contain tubes, including Mammoth Cave.

moments.title: Duck Creek Village
moments.text: Duck Creek Village sits at 8,507 feet on the edge of Cedar Mountain. Eastbound SR 14 passes Duck Creek Pond before the village, one of the few places with services along this mountain road. Farther east comes the turnoff for Mammoth Creek Road, connecting north to SR 143, before the byway descends into Long Valley.
